title: Tidal Bans AI-Generated Music
content:
The music streaming service Tidal said Tuesday that it would ban tracks it believes are completely AI-generated starting next month, a move its leader believes “will resonate with both artists and listeners alike.”
The service will remove the AI tracks starting Dec. 9, making Tidal the first music streaming platform to ban AI music entirely. It comes nearly five months after Tidal said it would demonetize any AI-powered song, force those artists to label their tracks as either AI-generated or AI-assisted and ban AI songs that were associated with “fraudulent activity,” a category that includes songs impersonating established artists and efforts to “deceive listeners.”
“But that’s enough, as 43% of tracks distributed to us in the last 90 days have been detected as AI-generated. Something more drastic needs to be done,” wrote Robert Andersen, the Tidal Lead at parent company Block, in an X thread on Tuesday. “We’ll begin removing all wholly AI-generated tracks from our catalog, and you’ll see them completely gone by the beginning of the year.”
Andersen said that 96% of all AI-generated songs receive zero plays. The move will cleave the platform of 29 million tracks, he added, and have it reject between 80,000 to 85,000 songs a day.
“We encourage our peers to follow suit,” he wrote.
The move comes as competitors such as Spotify and Apple Music continue to test approaches to combat the rise of AI-generated tracks proliferating on their platforms, many of which the services have labeled some version of “slop” or “spam.” Apple Music said it would also begin labeling AI-generated or AI-assisted tracks on its platform, while Spotify said it would label artists it deemed AI creations as an “AI Persona.”
Spotify said in a blog post last month it also removed 50 million slop or spam tracks from users’ recommendations this year, which came after it removed 75 million of those songs from its catalog entirely. The revelation came among a number of updates regarding Spotify’s efforts to combat AI spam.
“This work isn’t finished,” Spotify added. “AI moves fast, and bad actors adapt just as fast. But as AI makes music more abundant, we believe listeners will value human artistry even more. Our job is to make Spotify the place they find it.”

report.summary: Tidal will begin removing wholly AI-generated tracks on Dec. 9, becoming the first major streaming service to ban AI music outright.
report.background: Generative AI music tools have improved rapidly, flooding streaming platforms with cheap, high-volume tracks. Tidal had already demonetized AI-powered songs, required AI-generated or AI-assisted labels, and banned fraudulent uses such as artist impersonation. But the volume became unmanageable: Tidal says 43% of tracks distributed to it in the last 90 days were detected as AI-generated, while 96% of AI songs get zero plays. Competitors are taking different routes: Spotify has removed tens of millions of spam tracks and labels “AI Personas,” while Apple Music plans AI labels. Tidal’s move tests whether outright exclusion, rather than labeling or demonetization, can protect artist trust and listener experience.
key_points: Tidal will start removing wholly AI-generated tracks on Dec. 9 and expects them to be gone by early next year. It is the first major music streaming platform to ban AI-generated music entirely, rather than merely labeling or demonetizing it.

The scale is striking: Tidal says 43% of tracks distributed to it in the last 90 days were detected as AI-generated, and 96% of AI-generated songs receive zero plays. The company expects to remove about 29 million tracks and reject 80,000 to 85,000 songs a day.

Tidal previously tried milder measures: demonetizing AI-powered songs, forcing disclosure as AI-generated or AI-assisted, and banning AI tracks tied to fraud or impersonation. Executives say those steps were insufficient because AI-generated supply kept rising faster than moderation could handle.

Competitors are not matching the blanket ban. Spotify and Apple Music are testing labels, “AI Persona” tags, and spam removal, while Tidal is urging peers to follow its stricter approach. The split sets up a policy experiment over how streaming platforms should treat synthetic music.

Tidal’s definition matters: it targets “wholly AI-generated” tracks, not AI-assisted music. That leaves room for human-made songs using AI tools, but it also raises questions about detection accuracy, appeals, and false positives as platforms try to classify tracks at scale.
report.impact: For the AI music industry, Tidal’s ban is a distribution gatekeeper’s warning: synthetic tracks may win tools and demos but struggle to reach major streaming catalogs. It could push AI music toward licensed creation tools, niche platforms, or user-generated content, and boost demand for detection, watermarking, and provenance metadata. For developers, disclosure and human-in-the-loop workflows become more important, but detection errors and appeals remain risks. For regular users, catalogs may feel cleaner and more human-curated, though some experimental music will disappear. The bigger signal is that platforms are moving from labeling AI content to enforcing boundaries around it.
report.tools: There is no reliable standard open-source AI-music detector, so follow Tidal’s policy updates, Spotify’s “AI Persona” labeling, and Apple Music’s AI labels. For technical follow-up, explore audio watermarking, provenance standards such as C2PA-style content credentials, DDEX metadata practices, and open audio-classification models on Hugging Face, while treating detection claims cautiously.
